verbatim_anchor: Pavlov (1927): "Any external stimulus which is to become the signal in a conditioned reflex must overlap in point of time with the action of an unconditioned stimulus." In delay conditioning, the CS onset precedes US onset with temporal overlap, and this arrangement is the most effective for establishing classical conditioning.
old_anchor: Delay conditioning is a type of forward conditioning in which presentation of the conditioned stimulus precedes and overlaps presentation of the unconditioned stimulus, and it is the most effective method for establishing a conditioned response.
testable_fact: Delay conditioning, in which the CS onset precedes and temporally overlaps the US onset, is the most effective arrangement for establishing a classically conditioned response.

chapter_title: Schedules, Shaping, and the Fine-Tuning of Behavior
verbatim_anchor: Herrnstein, R.J. (1961). Relative and absolute strength of response as a function of frequency of reinforcement. Journal of the Experimental Analysis of Behavior, 4(3), 267-272: "The relative frequency of responding on a key equaled the relative frequency of reinforcement from it." The matching law states that the relative rate of responding on a particular alternative matches the relative rate of reinforcement obtained from that alternative. When two or more concurrent schedules operate simultaneously, the organism distributes its behavior proportionally to the reinforcement each schedule delivers.
old_anchor: The matching law predicts the effects of two or more concurrent schedules of reinforcement on the behaviors that are being reinforced.
testable_fact: Herrnstein's matching law states that an organism's relative rate of responding on concurrent schedules proportionally matches the relative rate of reinforcement obtained from each alternative.

chapter_title: The Architecture of Association: How Classical Conditioning Builds Learned Responses
verbatim_anchor: Rescorla, R.A. (1988). Pavlovian conditioning: It's not what you think it is. American Psychologist, 43(3), 151-160: "The previously neutral conditioned stimulus comes to elicit the response" after pairing with the unconditioned stimulus. "One, initially neutral in that it elicits no response, is called the conditioned stimulus (CS); the other, which is one that consistently elicits a response, is called the unconditioned stimulus (US)."
old_anchor: In classical conditioning research, the white rat was the conditioned stimulus, because it produced a startle response after being repeatedly paired with the unconditioned stimulus, an unexpected loud noise, which naturally elicited a startle response.
testable_fact: In classical conditioning, a neutral conditioned stimulus (CS) acquires the ability to elicit a conditioned response after repeated pairing with an unconditioned stimulus (US) that naturally elicits a response.

chapter_title: The Architecture of Association: How Classical Conditioning Builds Learned Responses
verbatim_anchor: Pavlov (1927): "If a tone of 1000 d.v. is established as a conditioned stimulus, many other tones spontaneously acquire similar properties, such properties diminishing proportionally to the intervals of these tones from the one of 1000 d.v." Stimuli resembling the original CS elicit the CR despite never being directly paired with the US.
old_anchor: Stimulus generalization occurs when stimuli similar to the original conditioned stimulus elicit the conditioned response without ever being presented with the unconditioned stimulus.
testable_fact: Stimulus generalization occurs when stimuli similar to the original CS elicit the conditioned response despite never being directly paired with the unconditioned stimulus.

chapter_title: The Architecture of Association: How Classical Conditioning Builds Learned Responses
verbatim_anchor: Pavlov (1927): "The hitherto quiet dog began to squeal in its stand, kept wriggling about, tore off with its teeth the apparatus for mechanical stimulation of the skin." "The clashing of excitation with inhibition led to a profound disturbance of the usual balance between these two processes." Experimental neurosis arises when an organism must discriminate between highly similar stimuli.
old_anchor: Pavlov's canine subjects exhibited "experimental neurosis" due to the requirement to make difficult discriminations between similar stimuli, which provoked agitation and aggression.
testable_fact: Pavlov's experimental neurosis arose in dogs required to make difficult discriminations between highly similar stimuli, producing agitation and disrupted behavior.

chapter_title: The Architecture of Association: How Classical Conditioning Builds Learned Responses

old_anchor: Little Albert's response to other white furry stimuli was due to stimulus generalization.

chapter_title: Beyond the Basics: Higher-Order Conditioning, Blocking, and Overshadowing
verbatim_anchor: Kamin, L.J. (1969). Predictability, surprise, attention, and conditioning. In B.A. Campbell & R.M. Church (Eds.), Punishment and aversive behavior (pp. 279-296): Prior conditioning to stimulus A "blocks" conditioning to stimulus B when both are presented as a compound AB paired with the US. The US must be "surprising" for new learning to occur. When the US is already fully predicted by the pre-trained CS, no additional associative strength accrues to the new stimulus presented simultaneously.
old_anchor: In classical conditioning, blocking occurs when a new neutral stimulus is simultaneously presented with a previously conditioned stimulus before presenting the unconditioned stimulus, preventing the new neutral stimulus from becoming a conditioned stimulus.
testable_fact: Kamin's blocking effect occurs when prior conditioning to stimulus A prevents new conditioning to stimulus B when AB is compounded with the US, because the US is no longer surprising.

chapter_title: Beyond the Basics: Higher-Order Conditioning, Blocking, and Overshadowing
verbatim_anchor: Mackintosh, N.J. (1976). Overshadowing and stimulus intensity. old_anchor: Testing the effects of overshadowing involves presenting two neutral stimuli together before the unconditioned stimulus, which leads to the less salient conditioned stimulus being overshadowed by the more salient one.
testable_fact: Overshadowing occurs when a more salient stimulus presented in compound with a less salient stimulus attenuates conditioning to the less salient stimulus.

chapter_title: Beyond the Basics: Higher-Order Conditioning, Blocking, and Overshadowing
verbatim_anchor: Rizley, R.C. & Rescorla, R.A. (1972). Associations in second-order conditioning and sensory preconditioning. CS2 elicits a CR even though it was never directly paired with the original US.
old_anchor: Pavlov's higher-order conditioning experiment involved pairing a tone with food so that the dog salivated when the tone was presented alone, and then pairing a light with the tone so that the dog also salivated when the light was presented alone.
testable_fact: In second-order conditioning, CS2 acquires the ability to elicit a conditioned response after being paired with CS1, even though CS2 was never directly paired with the original unconditioned stimulus.

chapter_title: Beyond the Basics: Higher-Order Conditioning, Blocking, and Overshadowing

chapter_title: Beyond the Basics: Higher-Order Conditioning, Blocking, and Overshadowing
verbatim_anchor: Pavlov (1927): Higher-order (second-order) conditioning involves first establishing a conditioned stimulus (CS1) by pairing it with an unconditioned stimulus, then pairing a new neutral stimulus (CS2) with the already-established CS1. "A well-established conditioned stimulus is used in the place of the unconditioned stimulus" so that CS2 also acquires the ability to elicit a conditioned response when presented alone, without ever having been directly paired with the unconditioned stimulus.
old_anchor: Higher-order conditioning involves treating the initial conditioned stimulus as an unconditioned stimulus and pairing it with a neutral stimulus so that the neutral stimulus also becomes a conditioned stimulus and elicits a conditioned response when presented alone.
testable_fact: In higher-order (second-order) conditioning, a new neutral stimulus (CS2) paired with an already-established CS1 acquires the ability to elicit a conditioned response without ever being directly paired with the unconditioned stimulus.

chapter_title: The Architecture of Association: How Classical Conditioning Builds Learned Responses
verbatim_anchor: Pavlov (1927): "Repeated application of a conditioned stimulus which is not followed up by reinforcement leads to a weakening of the conditioned reflex." "Left to themselves extinguished conditioned reflexes spontaneously recover their full strength after a longer or shorter interval of time." "It cannot be regarded as an irreparable destruction of the conditioned reflex... evidenced by the fact that the extinguished reflexes spontaneously regenerate in course of time." Extinction suppresses rather than eliminates learned associations.
old_anchor: Spontaneous recovery refers to the return of an extinguished conditioned response without the conditioned stimulus being presented again with the unconditioned stimulus, confirming that a conditioned response is suppressed rather than eliminated by extinction trials.
testable_fact: Spontaneous recovery — the return of an extinguished CR after a rest interval without reconditioning — demonstrates that extinction suppresses rather than permanently eliminates the learned association.

chapter_title: The Architecture of Association: How Classical Conditioning Builds Learned Responses

testable_fact: The conditioned response in classical conditioning is typically similar to but less intense than the unconditioned response.

chapter_title: Consequences That Shape Behavior: Reinforcement, Punishment, and the Operant Framework
verbatim_anchor: Thorndike (1911): Thorndike's research with cats in a puzzle box led to his development of the law of effect: "Of several responses made to the same situation, those which are accompanied or closely followed by satisfaction to the animal will, other things being equal, be more firmly connected with the situation... those which are accompanied or closely followed by discomfort to the animal will, other things being equal, have their connections with that situation weakened."
old_anchor: Thorndike's research with cats in a puzzle box led to his development of the law of effect.
testable_fact: Thorndike's law of effect states that responses followed by satisfying outcomes are strengthened while those followed by discomfort are weakened, derived from his puzzle-box research with cats.

chapter_title: Consequences That Shape Behavior: Reinforcement, Punishment, and the Operant Framework
verbatim_anchor: Dinsmoor, J.A. (1977). Escape, avoidance, punishment. Journal of the Experimental Analysis of Behavior, 28(1), 83-95: "More rapid termination of the shock selectively reinforced the behavior of holding the bar down." Escape conditioning is a form of negative reinforcement in which a behavior terminates an ongoing aversive stimulus.
old_anchor: Continuing to say "I love you" to his mother whenever she yells at the boy is a result of escape conditioning, where the behavior is maintained because it allows the boy to "escape" his mother's yelling.
testable_fact: Escape conditioning is a form of negative reinforcement in which a behavior is strengthened because it terminates an ongoing aversive stimulus.

chapter_title: Consequences That Shape Behavior: Reinforcement, Punishment, and the Operant Framework
verbatim_anchor: Skinner (1953): "We define the negative reinforcer (an aversive stimulus) as any stimulus the withdrawal of which strengthens the behavior." Behavior that terminates an aversive stimulus is strengthened by removal of that stimulus.
old_anchor: Negative reinforcement occurs when a behavior continues or increases because performing the behavior results in the termination or withdrawal of a stimulus, as exemplified by a woman who eats chocolate because it reduces her anxiety.
testable_fact: Negative reinforcement strengthens behavior by removing an aversive stimulus contingent upon that behavior.

chapter_title: Consequences That Shape Behavior: Reinforcement, Punishment, and the Operant Framework
verbatim_anchor: Moher, C.A. et al. (2008). Non-generalized and generalized conditioned reinforcers. Behavioral Interventions, 23(1), 13-38: Generalized conditioned reinforcers "may be less sensitive to the effects of satiation" because their effectiveness "does not depend on a single kind of deprivation." "Increasing the number of backup reinforcers with which the token was paired resulted in the effectiveness maintaining during satiation conditions."
old_anchor: Generalized reinforcers (e.g., money, tokens) are less susceptible than primary and secondary reinforcers to satiation because they can be exchanged for a variety of back-up (primary) reinforcers.
testable_fact: Generalized conditioned reinforcers (e.g., money, tokens) are less susceptible to satiation than primary reinforcers because their effectiveness depends on access to multiple backup reinforcers rather than a single deprivation state.

chapter_title: Consequences That Shape Behavior: Reinforcement, Punishment, and the Operant Framework
verbatim_anchor: Skinner, B.F. (1953). Science and human behavior. Macmillan: A positive discriminative stimulus (S^D) "sets the occasion" for a response by signaling that reinforcement is available. In its presence, the operant response is reinforced; in its absence, the response goes unreinforced. The S^D does not elicit the behavior but rather indicates that reinforcement is contingent upon the response.
old_anchor: A positive discriminative stimulus signals that a behavior will be reinforced.
testable_fact: A positive discriminative stimulus (S^D) signals that reinforcement is available for a response but does not elicit the behavior; it sets the occasion for the operant response.

chapter_title: Consequences That Shape Behavior: Reinforcement, Punishment, and the Operant Framework
verbatim_anchor: Lerman, D.C. & Vorndran, C.M. (2002). On the status of knowledge for using punishment. Journal of Applied Behavior Analysis, 35(4), 431-464: Negative punishment involves "the removal of stimuli, often called negative punishment (i.e., response cost, time-out from positive reinforcement)." The removal of a desirable stimulus following a behavior decreases the likelihood of that behavior occurring in the future.
old_anchor: Negative punishment occurs when a behavior decreases or stops because a stimulus is removed following the behavior, as in the situation where a 12-year-old boy stops teasing his younger sister because his parents subtract 50 cents from his weekly allowance whenever he does so.
testable_fact: Negative punishment decreases the future probability of a behavior by removing a desirable stimulus contingent upon that behavior.

chapter_title: Consequences That Shape Behavior: Reinforcement, Punishment, and the Operant Framework
verbatim_anchor: Mowrer, O.H. (1956). Two-factor learning theory reconsidered. Psychological Review, 63(2), 114-128: "Basically the two-factor, or two-process, hypothesis holds that habits are learned on the basis of the reinforcement provided by reward, or drive reduction, and that fears are learned (conditioned) on the basis of the contiguous occurrence of a signal and punishment." Avoidance involves (1) classical conditioning of fear to a neutral stimulus and (2) operant conditioning of avoidance behavior reinforced by fear reduction.
old_anchor: Mowrer's (1960) two-factor theory of learning proposes that avoidance conditioning is an example of two-factor learning because it combines classical conditioning and negative reinforcement (operant conditioning).
testable_fact: Mowrer's two-factor theory proposes that avoidance behavior involves classical conditioning of fear to a neutral stimulus and operant conditioning (negative reinforcement) in which avoidance is maintained by fear reduction.

chapter_title: Consequences That Shape Behavior: Reinforcement, Punishment, and the Operant Framework
verbatim_anchor: Mowrer, O.H. (1956). Two-factor learning theory reconsidered. Psychological Review, 63(2), 114-128: "Basically the two-factor, or two-process, hypothesis holds that habits are learned on the basis of the reinforcement provided by reward, or drive reduction, and that fears are learned (conditioned) on the basis of the contiguous occurrence of a signal and punishment." testable_fact: Mowrer's two-factor theory holds that avoidance conditioning combines classical conditioning of fear to a neutral cue and operant negative reinforcement in which the avoidance response is maintained by reducing conditioned fear.

chapter_title: Schedules, Shaping, and the Fine-Tuning of Behavior
verbatim_anchor: Reynolds, G.S. (1961). Behavioral contrast. Journal of the Experimental Analysis of Behavior, 4(1), 57-71: "The increase in the rate of responding during one component of a multiple schedule when the conditions in another component are changed so as to decrease the rate of responding during that component" constitutes behavioral contrast. When reinforcement is discontinued for one behavior but maintained for another, the still-reinforced behavior increases in rate -- a phenomenon termed behavioral contrast.
old_anchor: The boy's response to the change in reinforcement, where the point system is stopped for cleaning the cat box but not for taking out the garbage, is referred to as behavioral contrast.
testable_fact: Behavioral contrast occurs when discontinuing reinforcement for one behavior in a multiple schedule causes the rate of the still-reinforced behavior to increase above its original baseline level.

chapter_title: Schedules, Shaping, and the Fine-Tuning of Behavior
verbatim_anchor: Reynolds, G.S. (1961). Behavioral contrast. Journal of the Experimental Analysis of Behavior, 4(1), 57-71: Positive behavioral contrast occurs when reinforcement for one behavior in a multiple schedule is discontinued while reinforcement for the other behavior remains unchanged, resulting in the still-reinforced behavior increasing in rate above its original baseline level, while the no-longer-reinforced behavior decreases.
old_anchor: Positive behavioral contrast occurs when two behaviors are being reinforced and the reinforcement for one behavior is stopped while reinforcement for the other behavior stays the same, resulting in the behavior that is no longer reinforced decreasing and the behavior that is still receiving the same amount of reinforcement increasing.
testable_fact: Positive behavioral contrast occurs in multiple schedules when reinforcement for one behavior is discontinued, causing the rate of the still-reinforced behavior to increase above its original baseline.

chapter_title: Schedules, Shaping, and the Fine-Tuning of Behavior

testable_fact: Schedule thinning is the systematic, gradual transition from a dense (thick) to a lean (thin) reinforcement schedule until a practical terminal schedule is reached.

chapter_title: Applied Principles and the Bridge to Research Methods
verbatim_anchor: Reynolds, G.S. (1961). Behavioral contrast. testable_fact: Positive behavioral contrast occurs when reinforcement is discontinued for one of two concurrently reinforced responses, causing the still-reinforced response to increase in frequency.

verbatim_anchor: Dinsmoor, J.A. (1977). Escape, avoidance, punishment. chapter_title: The Architecture of Change: Readiness, Motivation, and Solution-Focused Practice
verbatim_anchor: Wolpe (1961): "In all instances, anxiety has been conditioned to situations in which, objectively, there is no danger." old_anchor: The use of in vivo exposure to treat a specific phobia is based on the assumption that the feared object or situation is a conditioned stimulus.
testable_fact: In vivo exposure for specific phobia rests on the classical conditioning assumption that the feared object or situation has become a conditioned stimulus eliciting anxiety through prior association with an aversive event.

old_anchor: Implosive therapy uses classical extinction to eliminate a fear response to an object or situation.
testable_fact: Implosive therapy eliminates fear responses through classical extinction via prolonged imaginal exposure to the feared stimulus presented at maximum intensity.

chapter_title: Building Behavior from the Ground Up: Operant Interventions in Clinical Practice

old_anchor: Overcorrection is ordinarily classified as a type of positive punishment.
testable_fact: Overcorrection is classified as positive punishment because it involves applying an effortful aversive consequence contingent upon occurrence of the undesired behavior.

chapter_title: The Architecture of Change: Readiness, Motivation, and Solution-Focused Practice
verbatim_anchor: Peterson (2004): Skinner described shaping as reinforcing "any response which had the slightest resemblance to a swipe — perhaps, at first, merely the behavior of looking at the ball — and then to select responses which more closely approximated the final form." "We had shaped a very complex topography of behavior through successive approximation in a matter of minutes."
old_anchor: The technique used by the mother to teach a young child with autism spectrum disorder to wave good-bye is known as shaping, which involves reinforcing successive approximations to the desired behavior until the desired behavior is established.
testable_fact: Shaping, as described by Skinner, involves reinforcing successive approximations to a desired behavior, gradually selecting responses that more closely resemble the final target behavior.

chapter_title: Building Behavior from the Ground Up: Operant Interventions in Clinical Practice
verbatim_anchor: Lerman & Iwata (1996): "Operant extinction is generally contraindicated when the target behavior poses a risk of harm, because extinction typically produces an initial increase in frequency and intensity (extinction burst) before the behavior decreases."
old_anchor: Of the interventions listed, operant extinction is the least likely to be the optimal intervention when a child's target behavior is harmful to him/herself or others because it often causes an increase in the behavior before it begins to decrease.
testable_fact: Operant extinction is contraindicated when a target behavior is harmful because it typically produces an extinction burst — an initial increase in frequency and intensity — before the behavior decreases.

chapter_title: Building Behavior from the Ground Up: Operant Interventions in Clinical Practice
verbatim_anchor: Peterson (2004): Skinner wrote that "elaborate and peculiar forms of response may be generated from undifferentiated operant behavior through successive approximation to a final form." The method involves reinforcing "upon the following steps in succession: approach to the site of the lever, lifting the nose into the air toward the lever, lifting the fore-part of the body into the air, touching the lever with the feet, and pressing the lever downward."
old_anchor: Shaping is also known as successive approximation conditioning, a behavioral technique that involves reinforcing successive approximations to the desired behavior.
testable_fact: Shaping, also called successive approximation conditioning, involves reinforcing progressively closer approximations to a desired final behavior until that behavior is established.

chapter_title: The Architecture of Change: Readiness, Motivation, and Solution-Focused Practice
verbatim_anchor: Foxx & Azrin (1973): "Overcorrection consists of two components: restitution (restoring the environment to its pre-behavior state or better) and positive practice (repeatedly performing the correct alternative behavior)."
old_anchor: Overcorrection, which is used to reduce or eliminate an undesirable behavior, consists of restitution (fixing any negative consequences) and positive practice (practicing more appropriate behaviors).
testable_fact: Overcorrection consists of two components: restitution (restoring the environment to its prior or better state) and positive practice (repeatedly performing the correct alternative behavior).

chapter_title: Building Behavior from the Ground Up: Operant Interventions in Clinical Practice
verbatim_anchor: Vollmer, Peters, Kronfli, Lloveras, & Ibanez (2020): "We propose the following definition of DRA: Providing greater reinforcement, along at least one dimension, contingent on the occurrence of one form or type of behavior, while minimizing reinforcement for another form or type of behavior." The over-arching suggestion "is to maximize reinforcement for alternative behavior and minimize or eliminate reinforcement for problem behavior."
old_anchor: Differential reinforcement combines positive reinforcement and operant extinction.
testable_fact: Differential reinforcement combines positive reinforcement for a target alternative behavior with extinction (minimizing or eliminating reinforcement) for the problem behavior.

chapter_title: Building Behavior from the Ground Up: Operant Interventions in Clinical Practice
verbatim_anchor: Premack (1959): The Premack principle states that a high-probability (preferred) behavior can be used as a reinforcer for a low-probability (less preferred) behavior. For a student who dislikes homework but enjoys other activities, making access to the preferred activity contingent on homework completion increases the rate of the low-frequency behavior.
old_anchor: The Premack principle, a type of positive reinforcement in which a high-frequency behavior (a highly desirable activity) is used as a reinforcer for a low-frequency behavior (an undesirable activity) to increase the low-frequency behavior, is useful for helping a middle school student who rarely finishes his homework just because he doesn't like doing it.
testable_fact: The Premack principle states that a high-probability preferred behavior can reinforce a low-probability less-preferred behavior, increasing its frequency when access to the preferred activity is made contingent on performing the less preferred one.

chapter_title: Rewiring Fear: How Classical Conditioning Principles Treat Anxiety
verbatim_anchor: Wolpe (1961): Systematic desensitization involves "presenting to the imagination of the deeply relaxed patient the feeblest item in a list of anxiety-evoking stimuli -- repeatedly, until no more anxiety is evoked." Systematic desensitization operates through counterconditioning -- replacing the anxiety response with an incompatible relaxation response -- while exposure therapy operates through extinction, in which repeated presentation of the feared stimulus without the aversive outcome weakens the conditioned fear response.
old_anchor: Systematic desensitization is counterconditioning, while exposure therapy is extinction.
testable_fact: Systematic desensitization operates through counterconditioning — replacing anxiety with an incompatible relaxation response — whereas exposure therapy operates through extinction of the conditioned fear response.

chapter_title: Building Behavior from the Ground Up: Operant Interventions in Clinical Practice
verbatim_anchor: Premack (1959): "A high-frequency (preferred) behavior can serve as a reinforcer to increase engagement in a low-frequency (less preferred) behavior."
old_anchor: The Premack principle, where a high-frequency behavior is used as a reinforcer for a low-frequency behavior, is used when a father tells his son he can play video games only after he finishes his homework.
testable_fact: The Premack principle holds that a high-frequency preferred behavior (e.g., video games) can serve as a reinforcer to increase a low-frequency less-preferred behavior (e.g., homework completion).

chapter_title: Building Behavior from the Ground Up: Operant Interventions in Clinical Practice
verbatim_anchor: Kazdin (1972): "Response cost (RC), a punishment procedure in which conditioned reinforcers (points, tokens, or money) are withdrawn to suppress a response, has been used as a behavior therapy technique on its own and in conjunction with reinforcement in token economies." "RC is a punishment procedure, i.e., the contingent presentation of a noxious stimulus which reduces the future probability of a response."
old_anchor: Response cost is an application of negative punishment, which reduces or eliminates a behavior by removing a positive reinforcer whenever the behavior occurs.
testable_fact: Response cost is a negative punishment procedure in which conditioned reinforcers such as points, tokens, or money are withdrawn contingent on an undesired behavior to reduce its future probability.

chapter_title: Building Behavior from the Ground Up: Operant Interventions in Clinical Practice
verbatim_anchor: Azrin & Holz (1966): "Habituation to the punishing stimulus is one mechanism by which punishment loses effectiveness over time, as repeated exposure reduces the aversive quality of the consequence."
old_anchor: Habituation is one of the reasons why punishment tends to become less effective over time.
testable_fact: Habituation to a punishing stimulus — whereby repeated exposure reduces its aversive quality — is one mechanism by which punishment loses effectiveness over time.

chapter_title: Building Behavior from the Ground Up: Operant Interventions in Clinical Practice
verbatim_anchor: Foxx & Azrin (1973): "Implementation of overcorrection may require verbal prompts and/or physical guidance to ensure the individual performs both the restitution and positive practice components."
old_anchor: Using the overcorrection technique to alter a child's undesirable behavior may require providing the child with verbal instructions and/or physical guidance.
testable_fact: Foxx and Azrin's overcorrection technique, which requires performance of both restitution and positive practice components, may necessitate verbal prompts and/or physical guidance to ensure correct implementation.

chapter_title: Before the Crisis: Prevention Science, Research Bias, and the Early Architecture of Therapeutic Change
verbatim_anchor: Cooper, Heron, & Heward (2020): "Chaining establishes a complex behavioral sequence of discrete responses in a fixed order. This differs from shaping, which builds a single behavior through successive approximations rather than linking component responses."
old_anchor: Chaining is used to establish a complex behavior that consists of a sequence of responses that occur in a fixed order, in contrast to shaping, which is used to establish a behavior by reinforcing successive approximations to (not components of) the behavior.
testable_fact: Chaining establishes a complex behavioral sequence of discrete responses in a fixed order, whereas shaping builds a single target behavior through successive approximations to that behavior.

chapter_title: Building Behavior from the Ground Up: Operant Interventions in Clinical Practice
verbatim_anchor: Cooper, Heron, & Heward (2020): "Task analysis — decomposing a target behavior into its component steps — is the requisite first step when implementing chaining. Forward chaining teaches from the first step; backward chaining starts with the last step."
old_anchor: Task analysis is the essential first step when using chaining, an intervention to establish a new behavior that consists of separate responses (links in the behavior chain) and involves teaching the individual how to perform each response in the behavior chain sequentially, starting with the first or the last response.
testable_fact: Task analysis is the essential first step in chaining, decomposing a target behavior into component steps that are then taught sequentially via either forward chaining (first step first) or backward chaining (last step first).

chapter_title: Rewiring Fear: How Classical Conditioning Principles Treat Anxiety
verbatim_anchor: Shapiro (2002): "The Adaptive Information Processing (AIP) model, which guides EMDR clinical practice, proposes that there is within each of us a physiological information-processing system in which new information is processed generally to an adaptive state." "It is hypothesized that the eye movements and other dual-attention stimuli enhance information processing."
old_anchor: As conceptualized by Shapiro and her colleagues, the rapid eye movement component of eye movement desensitization and reprocessing exerts its beneficial effects on the symptoms of PTSD by accelerating information processing and adaptive resolution of traumatic memories.
testable_fact: Shapiro's Adaptive Information Processing model proposes that EMDR's dual-attention stimuli, including eye movements, facilitate processing of traumatic memories to an adaptive resolution.

chapter_title: Building Behavior from the Ground Up: Operant Interventions in Clinical Practice
verbatim_anchor: Premack (1959): The Premack principle is based on the assumption that behaviors can be ordered by their probability of occurrence and that more probable (higher-frequency) behaviors can serve as reinforcers for less probable (lower-frequency) behaviors. This principle redefines reinforcement in terms of response probabilities rather than stimulus properties.
old_anchor: The Premack principle is based on the assumption that high probability behaviors can be used to increase low probability behaviors.
testable_fact: The Premack principle holds that higher-probability behaviors can serve as reinforcers for lower-probability behaviors, redefining reinforcement in terms of response probabilities rather than stimulus properties.

chapter_title: Culturally Responsive Practice: Therapeutic Adaptations and Client Preferences
verbatim_anchor: Ridley (1984): "Healthy cultural paranoia describes a Black client's adaptive mistrust of White therapists and institutions, reflecting a realistic appraisal of historical and ongoing racism rather than psychopathology. A Black client who withholds personal information from a White therapist may be exhibiting a culturally appropriate self-protective response." Context: Ridley distinguished healthy cultural paranoia from pathological paranoia, arguing that clinicians must recognize that cultural mistrust in interracial therapy dyads is a rational response to racism rather than a symptom of mental illness.
old_anchor: Ridley's concept of "healthy cultural paranoia" is useful for understanding why a Black therapy client may resist disclosing personal information to a White therapist.
testable_fact: Ridley's healthy cultural paranoia describes Black clients' adaptive, reality-based mistrust of White therapists as a culturally appropriate self-protective response to racism rather than psychopathology.

chapter_title: Navigating Two Worlds: Acculturation, Minority Stress, and Worldview
verbatim_anchor: Ward & Kennedy (1993): "Cultural fit refers to the degree of congruence between an immigrant's personality characteristics and personal attributes and the cultural values and behavioral norms of the host society. Greater cultural fit is associated with more successful psychological and sociocultural adaptation." Context: Research on acculturation outcomes consistently shows that immigrants whose personal traits align with host-culture expectations experience less acculturative stress and better adjustment.
old_anchor: Cultural fit refers to how well an immigrant's personality and other personal attributes match the cultural values and norms of the host country.
testable_fact: Cultural fit refers to the degree of congruence between an immigrant's personality and personal attributes and the cultural values and norms of the host society, with greater fit associated with better adaptation.

chapter_title: Navigating Two Worlds: Acculturation, Minority Stress, and Worldview
verbatim_anchor: Verkuyten (2016): "The integration paradox is the counterintuitive finding that higher-status immigrants -- those with greater education and economic achievement -- report more perceived discrimination and a lower sense of belonging to the host society than lower-status immigrants." Context: Higher-educated immigrants may have greater awareness of discrimination, higher expectations for equal treatment, and more frequent contact with mainstream institutions where discrimination occurs, paradoxically increasing their perception of exclusion.
old_anchor: The integration paradox refers to the observation that higher-status immigrants (i.e., those with higher levels of education and economic success) are more likely than lower-status immigrants to report experiencing discrimination and having a low sense of belonging to the host society.
testable_fact: The integration paradox is the counterintuitive finding that higher-status, better-educated immigrants report more perceived discrimination and lower sense of belonging to the host society than lower-status immigrants.

chapter_title: Foundations of Culture: Etic, Emic, and Communication Across Cultures
verbatim_anchor: Gelfand et al. (2011): "Tight cultures have strong social norms and low tolerance for deviant behavior, whereas loose cultures have weak social norms and high tolerance for deviant behavior. The strength of social norms and the degree of sanctioning within societies represent a core dimension of cross-cultural variation." Context: Gelfand and colleagues demonstrated that tightness-looseness is shaped by ecological and historical threats (e.g., natural disasters, disease prevalence, territorial conflicts) that necessitate strong norms for social coordination and survival.
old_anchor: The factors that determine whether a culture is "tight" or "loose" are the strength of social norms and tolerance for deviance, where tight cultures have strong social norms and low tolerance for deviant behaviors, while loose cultures have weak social norms and high tolerance for deviant behaviors.
testable_fact: Tight cultures have strong social norms and low tolerance for deviant behavior, while loose cultures have weak social norms and high tolerance for deviance, with tightness shaped by historical and ecological threats.

chapter_title: The Wounds of Racism: Internalized Oppression, Microaggressions, and Bias

old_anchor: Assigning a level of intelligence to a person of color on the basis of the person's race is a type of microinsult, as described by Sue et al. (2007).
testable_fact: Microinsult, as described by Sue et al. (2007), involves verbal or behavioral communications conveying stereotypical assumptions based on group membership, such as ascribing intelligence level based on race.

chapter_title: Navigating Two Worlds: Acculturation, Minority Stress, and Worldview
verbatim_anchor: Meyer (2003): "Minority stress theory provides a conceptual framework for understanding how the excess stress experienced by members of stigmatized minority groups -- arising from prejudice, discrimination, and stigma -- creates chronic psychological strain and heightened physiological arousal that adversely affect mental and physical health over time." Context: Meyer distinguished between distal stressors (external events such as discrimination and violence) and proximal stressors (internalized processes such as expectations of rejection and concealment of identity).
old_anchor: Minority stress theory provides a framework for conceptualizing how experiences unique to minority groups - prejudice and discrimination, in particular - confer chronic psychological stress and heightened physiological responses that impact mental and physical health over time.
testable_fact: Meyer's minority stress theory distinguishes distal stressors (e.g., discrimination) from proximal stressors (e.g., internalized stigma, expectations of rejection), both of which create chronic strain that adversely affects minority group members' mental and physical health.

chapter_title: Culturally Responsive Practice: Therapeutic Adaptations and Client Preferences
verbatim_anchor: Sue & Sue (2016) / Thompson, Bazile, & Akbar (2004): Research suggests that African American therapy clients are most likely to prefer an egalitarian, problem-focused, and time-limited approach to therapy. This preference reflects cultural values emphasizing directness, practical outcomes, and collaborative (rather than hierarchically structured) therapeutic relationships.
old_anchor: African American therapy clients are most likely to prefer an egalitarian, problem-focused, time-limited approach.
testable_fact: African American therapy clients are most likely to prefer an egalitarian, problem-focused, and time-limited therapeutic approach reflecting cultural values of directness, practical outcomes, and collaborative relationships.

chapter_title: Identity in Development: Cross, Helms, Atkinson, and Racial Identity Models
verbatim_anchor: Cross (1971) / Atkinson, Morten, & Sue (1998): The initial stage of most racial/ethnic identity development models is characterized by disinterest in or rejection of one's own racial/ethnic identity. In Cross's model, this is the pre-encounter stage, where the individual holds pro-White/majority culture attitudes and places little emphasis on racial identity. In the Atkinson, Morten, and Sue model, this corresponds to the conformity stage.
old_anchor: The initial stage of most racial/ethnic identity development models is characterized by disinterest in or rejection of one's own racial/ethnic identity.
testable_fact: The initial stage of most racial/ethnic identity development models is characterized by disinterest in or rejection of one's own racial/ethnic identity, corresponding to Cross's pre-encounter stage and Atkinson, Morten, and Sue's conformity stage.

chapter_title: Foundations of Culture: Etic, Emic, and Communication Across Cultures
verbatim_anchor: Hall (1976): "In high-context cultures, communication depends heavily on the surrounding context, shared group knowledge, and nonverbal cues; the meaning is embedded in the situation rather than in the explicit verbal message. Knowledge acquisition in high-context cultures is similarly situation-dependent." Context: Hall contrasted high-context cultures (e.g., Japanese, Chinese, Arab) with low-context cultures (e.g., German, Scandinavian, American), noting that high-context communication relies on implicit, nonverbal channels while low-context communication relies on direct verbal expression.
old_anchor: For members of cultural groups that emphasize high-context communication, knowledge depends largely on the nature of the situation and communication relies primarily on nonverbal messages.
testable_fact: In Hall's framework, high-context cultures rely heavily on situational context, shared group knowledge, and nonverbal cues for communication rather than explicit verbal messages.

chapter_title: Foundations of Culture: Etic, Emic, and Communication Across Cultures
verbatim_anchor: Morris, Leung, Ames, & Lickel (1999): "The emic or inside perspective follows in the tradition of psychological studies of folk beliefs and in cultural anthropologists' striving to understand culture from 'the native's point of view.' The etic or outside perspective follows in the tradition of comparativist researchers." A psychotherapist with an emic perspective recognizes the differences between cultural groups and tailors assessment and intervention to be culturally specific.
old_anchor: A psychotherapist who has an emic perspective recognizes the differences between cultural groups.
testable_fact: A therapist with an emic perspective recognizes differences between cultural groups and tailors assessment and intervention to be culturally specific rather than applying universal frameworks.

chapter_title: The Wounds of Racism: Internalized Oppression, Microaggressions, and Bias

They can interact in such a way as to form four quadrants: IC-IR, EC-IR, EC-ER, and IC-ER." A Black therapy client with an IC-ER worldview (internal control, external responsibility -- attributing problems to systemic forces) is likely to be the most challenging for a White middle-class therapist with an IC-IR worldview (internal control, internal responsibility -- attributing outcomes to individual effort).
old_anchor: A Black therapy client with an IC-ER worldview is likely to be the most challenging for a White middle-class therapist with an IC-IR worldview.
testable_fact: A Black client with an IC-ER worldview (internal control, external responsibility) is likely to be most challenging for a White middle-class therapist holding an IC-IR worldview (internal control, internal responsibility), as described by Sue (1978).

chapter_title: Foundations of Culture: Etic, Emic, and Communication Across Cultures

The strong norms and low tolerance for deviance in tight cultures promote orderliness and self-discipline while discouraging novelty-seeking and unconventional behavior." chapter_title: Identity in Development: Cross, Helms, Atkinson, and Racial Identity Models

old_anchor: The first stages of Atkinson, Morten, and Sue's Racial/Cultural Identity Development Model and Cross's Black Racial Identity Development Model are characterized by positive attitudes toward White (majority) culture and negative attitudes toward Black (minority) culture.
testable_fact: The conformity stage of Atkinson, Morten, and Sue's model and the pre-encounter stage of Cross's Black Racial Identity model are both characterized by positive attitudes toward White majority culture and negative attitudes toward one's own minority culture.

chapter_title: Becoming Multicultural: Sue's Framework, Competence, and Integration
verbatim_anchor: Sellers, Smith, Shelton, Rowley, & Chavous (1998): "In the Multidimensional Model of Racial Identity (MMRI), racial salience -- the extent to which race is a relevant part of one's self-concept at a particular moment -- is influenced by both the individual's level of racial centrality and the characteristics of the current situation." old_anchor: Racial salience is affected by the current situation and racial centrality in Seller et al.'s (1998) multidimensional model of racial identity.
testable_fact: In Sellers et al.'s MMRI, racial salience is dynamic and context-dependent, influenced by both the situation and the individual's relatively stable level of racial centrality.

chapter_title: Identity in Development: Cross, Helms, Atkinson, and Racial Identity Models
verbatim_anchor: Bishop, Fish, Hammack, & Russell (2020): "The Generations Study was a five-year longitudinal study examining the health and well-being of lesbian, gay, and bisexual individuals across three age cohorts (18-25, 34-41, and 52-59). Consistent with previous research on accelerating sexual identity development milestones, the youngest cohort reported the earliest ages of first experiencing all five milestones, while the oldest cohort reported the latest ages. The five milestones studied were: awareness of same-sex attraction, LGB self-identification, same-sex sexual behavior, disclosure to a straight friend, and disclosure to a family member." Context: The generational differences in milestone timing reflect broad societal shifts including greater acceptance, legal protections, and media representation of LGB identities that have created more supportive contexts for earlier identity development.
old_anchor: The Generations Study was a five-year study that examined the health and well-being of lesbian, gay, and bisexual (LGB) individuals who represented three age cohorts: 18-25, 34-41, and 52-59. Included in this study were questions about participants' ages when they first experienced five sexual identity milestones: awareness of same-sex attraction; self-identification as lesbian, gay, or bisexual; same-sex sexual behavior; disclosure as a sexual minority to a straight friend; and disclosure as a sexual minority to a family member. Consistent with previous research, Bishop, Fish, Hammack, and Russell found that members of the younger cohort reported first experiencing all milestones at the youngest ages, while members of the older cohort reported first experiencing all milestones at the oldest ages.
testable_fact: The Generations Study found that younger LGB cohorts reported earlier ages at all five sexual identity milestones — awareness, self-identification, same-sex behavior, and disclosure to friend and family — reflecting increasingly supportive societal contexts.

chapter_title: The Wounds of Racism: Internalized Oppression, Microaggressions, and Bias
verbatim_anchor:
Meissner & Brigham (2001): "The own-race bias (cross-race effect) is the robust finding that facial recognition accuracy is higher for same-race faces than for other-race faces."
