Jones & Nisbett (1971): "The actor-observer bias is the pattern whereby individuals attribute their own actions to situational pressures but attribute identical actions by others to dispositional traits."
**[MONOGRAPH/BOOK CHAPTER -- Jones, E. E., & Nisbett, R. E. (1971). The actor and the observer: Divergent perceptions of the causes of behavior. In E. E. Jones et al. (Eds.), Attribution: Perceiving the Causes of Behavior (pp. 79-94). Morristown, NJ: General Learning Press. PDF on LaCie (DOI 10.1037/0033-2909.101.1.75) contained wrong article (Funder, 1987, about accuracy in social judgment). Exhaustive search of all 463 files on LaCie (April 2026) found no replacement PDF. Content is the foundational actor-observer attribution distinction. RETAINED -- book chapter source, no journal replacement available on LaCie.]**
old_anchor: A friend tends to attribute their own behaviors to situational factors but the behaviors of other people to dispositional factors, illustrating the actor-observer bias.
testable_fact: The actor-observer bias is the tendency for individuals to attribute their own behavior to situational factors while attributing identical behavior by others to dispositional traits.

chapter_title: How We Are Moved: Persuasion, Social Influence, and Compliance
verbatim_anchor: McGuire (1964): "The attitude inoculation hypothesis proposes that pre-exposing individuals to a weakened form of a counterargument, along with refutations of that argument, builds resistance to subsequent stronger persuasive attacks -- analogous to biological immunization. A refutational defense, in which the individual practices countering weak opposing arguments, is more effective at building persuasion resistance than a supportive defense that merely reinforces the original attitude." Context: McGuire's inoculation theory was developed primarily to address cultural truisms (widely accepted beliefs that individuals have never had to defend), demonstrating that rehearsing counterargument refutation creates a psychological 'antibody' against future persuasion attempts.
old_anchor: McGuire's attitude inoculation hypothesis addresses the usefulness of a refutational defense for increasing resistance to persuasion.
testable_fact: McGuire's inoculation theory proposes that exposure to weakened counterarguments with refutations builds resistance to later persuasion, and a refutational defense is more effective than a supportive defense for this purpose.

chapter_title: How We Judge: Attribution Theory, Biases, and Causal Explanations
verbatim_anchor:
Gilbert & Malone (1995): "The correspondence bias is the tendency to draw inferences about a person's unique and enduring dispositions from behaviors that can be entirely explained by the situations in which they occur."
**[JOURNAL -- Gilbert, D. T., & Malone, P. S. (1995). The correspondence bias. Psychological Bulletin, 117(1), 21-38. PDF verified on LaCie. Replaced book chapter with definitive journal review of the construct Ross (1977) introduced. CORRECT.]**
old_anchor: The fundamental attribution error is the tendency to overestimate the role of dispositional factors and underestimate the role of situational factors when making attributions about the behaviors of other people.
testable_fact: Gilbert and Malone's correspondence bias is the tendency to infer stable personal dispositions from others' behaviors even when those behaviors are fully explained by situational factors.

chapter_title: How We Judge: Attribution Theory, Biases, and Causal Explanations
verbatim_anchor: Karau & Williams (1993): "Social loafing is most likely to have a detrimental effect on team performance when the team is large and only the total group output (rather than individual contributions) is assessed. Under these conditions, individual accountability is low and the diffusion of responsibility is maximized." Context: The collective effort model (Karau & Williams, 1993) predicts that individuals reduce effort in group settings when they perceive that their individual contributions are dispensable, unidentifiable, or not subject to evaluation.
old_anchor: When forming a work team to complete an important project, social loafing is most likely to have a negative effect on the team's performance when the team is large and only the total group performance will be assessed.
testable_fact: Social loafing is most detrimental to team performance when the group is large and only total group output is assessed, conditions that minimize individual accountability and maximize diffusion of responsibility.

chapter_title: The Power of the Situation: Conformity, Obedience, and Group Dynamics
verbatim_anchor: Batson (1991): "Altruistic motivation -- helping driven by genuine concern for improving the victim's well-being -- is more predictive of sustained future helping behavior than egoistic motivation, which is driven primarily by the desire to alleviate one's own distress at witnessing suffering." Context: Batson's empathy-altruism hypothesis posits that empathic concern produces truly altruistic motivation directed toward the welfare of others, as distinct from personal distress, which produces egoistic motivation aimed at reducing one's own aversive emotional state.
old_anchor: Altruistic motivation (helping to improve the victims' well-being) for helping victims of a tragedy was more predictive than egoistic motivation (helping to alleviate one's own suffering) for predicting future helping.
testable_fact: Batson's empathy-altruism hypothesis holds that altruistic motivation—helping to improve a victim's welfare—is more predictive of future helping than egoistic motivation aimed at reducing one's own distress.

chapter_title: What We Believe: Attitudes, Cognitive Dissonance, and Self-Perception
verbatim_anchor:
Miller & Ross (1975): "The self-serving bias is the tendency to credit personal successes to internal dispositions while blaming failures on external circumstances."
**[JOURNAL -- Psychological Bulletin, 82(2), 213-225. Content verified. CORRECT.]**
old_anchor: The self-serving bias is the tendency to attribute our successes to dispositional factors and our failures to situational factors.
testable_fact: The self-serving bias is the tendency to attribute personal successes to internal dispositional factors and failures to external situational factors.

chapter_title: Culturally Responsive Practice: Therapeutic Adaptations and Client Preferences
verbatim_anchor: Langer (1975): "Illusory control is the mistaken belief that one can influence outcomes determined by chance. Gamblers frequently exhibit illusory control by engaging in superstitious rituals (e.g., blowing on dice, wearing a 'lucky' item) under the belief that these actions can alter random outcomes." Context: Langer identified several factors that increase illusory control, including active involvement in the task, competition, familiarity with the stimulus, and choice -- all of which introduce skill-relevant cues into chance situations.
old_anchor: Gamblers may exhibit illusory control, which is the belief that certain superstitious objects or rituals (e.g., blowing on dice) can alter outcomes, especially outcomes that are random or due to chance.
testable_fact: Langer's illusory control is the mistaken belief that one can influence chance-determined outcomes, commonly demonstrated by gamblers who engage in superstitious rituals to alter random events.

chapter_title: The Power of the Situation: Conformity, Obedience, and Group Dynamics
verbatim_anchor:
Deutsch & Gerard (1955): "Informational influence -- conforming because others' judgments are taken as evidence of reality -- tends to exceed normative influence when the task is ambiguous and difficult."
**[JOURNAL -- Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology, 51(3), 629-636. Verified on PubMed (PMID: 13286010). Content verified. CORRECT.]**
old_anchor: Informational influence is usually stronger than normative influence when the task is ambiguous and difficult.
testable_fact: Deutsch and Gerard found that informational influence—conforming because others' judgments serve as evidence of reality—tends to exceed normative influence when tasks are ambiguous and difficult.

chapter_title: What We Believe: Attitudes, Cognitive Dissonance, and Self-Perception
verbatim_anchor:
Rosenstock (1974): "The Health Belief Model identifies perceived susceptibility, perceived severity, perceived benefits, perceived barriers, cues to action, and self-efficacy as determinants of health behavior -- behavioral norms are not included."
**[JOURNAL -- Health Education Monographs, 2(4), 354-386. CONTENT NOTE: Self-efficacy was not part of the original 1974 HBM; it was added later by Rosenstock, Strecher, & Becker (1988). The original 1974 model included susceptibility, severity, benefits, and barriers. Cues to action were also added in subsequent revisions. The content is correct as a description of the current/expanded HBM but anachronistic for 1974.]**
old_anchor: The Health Belief Model does not identify behavioral norms as a factor contributing to the likelihood that a person will engage in behaviors that reduce the risk for developing a disorder.
testable_fact: The Health Belief Model includes perceived susceptibility, severity, benefits, barriers, cues to action, and self-efficacy as determinants of health behavior, but does not include behavioral norms.

chapter_title: The Power of the Situation: Conformity, Obedience, and Group Dynamics
verbatim_anchor: Darley & Latane (1968): "The bystander effect describes the finding that the probability of an individual providing help decreases as the number of bystanders increases. Latane and Darley used this phenomenon to explain the failure of witnesses to intervene during the 1964 murder of Kitty Genovese in New York City." Context: Darley and Latane identified three psychological mechanisms underlying the bystander effect: diffusion of responsibility (each bystander feels less personal obligation to act), pluralistic ignorance (bystanders look to others' inaction as a signal that help is unnecessary), and evaluation apprehension (fear of being judged negatively for intervening).
old_anchor: Latane and Darley (1970) used the bystander effect to explain the murder of Kitty Genovese in New York in 1964.
testable_fact: Darley and Latane's bystander effect holds that the probability of helping decreases as the number of bystanders increases, explained by diffusion of responsibility, pluralistic ignorance, and evaluation apprehension.

chapter_title: How We Judge: Attribution Theory, Biases, and Causal Explanations
verbatim_anchor:
Allison & Messick (1985): "The group attribution error is the tendency to assume that an individual group member's attitudes or behaviors reflect the attitudes of the entire group."
**[JOURNAL -- Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 21(6), 563-579. Content verified. CORRECT.]**
old_anchor: The tendency to believe that the personal attitudes of a member of a group are similar to the personal attitudes of all members of the group is referred to as the group attribution error.
testable_fact: The group attribution error is the tendency to assume that an individual group member's attitudes or behaviors reflect those of the entire group.

chapter_title: How We Judge: Attribution Theory, Biases, and Causal Explanations
verbatim_anchor:
Pettigrew (1979): "The ultimate attribution error extends attributional bias to the group level: positive outgroup behaviors are dismissed as situational, while negative outgroup behaviors are attributed to dispositional qualities, with the inverse pattern for the ingroup."
**[JOURNAL -- Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 5(4), 461-476. Content verified. CORRECT.]**
old_anchor: The ultimate attribution error applies to attributions made about members of an entire group, where members of an in-group consistently attribute the negative outcomes of out-group members to dispositional factors and their positive outcomes to situational factors.
testable_fact: Pettigrew's ultimate attribution error extends attributional bias to the group level, with negative outgroup behaviors attributed dispositionally and positive outgroup behaviors dismissed as situational, with the reverse pattern for the ingroup.

chapter_title: How We Judge: Attribution Theory, Biases, and Causal Explanations
verbatim_anchor: Jones & Nisbett (1971): "The actor-observer effect predicts that actors tend to attribute their own behaviors to situational factors (e.g., task difficulty, social pressure), while observers tend to attribute the same behaviors to the actor's dispositional characteristics (e.g., personality traits, abilities). Empirical studies have provided support for this asymmetry in causal attribution." Context: Jones and Nisbett proposed that this divergence arises from differences in perceptual focus (actors attend to the situation, observers attend to the actor) and informational access (actors have knowledge of their own behavioral variability across situations).
old_anchor: This study provided support for the actor-observer effect, which predicts that actors tend to attribute their own behaviors to situational factors while observers tend to attribute them to dispositional factors.
testable_fact: The actor-observer effect predicts that actors attribute their own behavior to situational factors while observers attribute the same behavior to the actor's dispositional characteristics, arising from differences in perceptual focus and informational access.

chapter_title: How We Judge: Attribution Theory, Biases, and Causal Explanations
verbatim_anchor: Ross (1977): "The fundamental attribution error is illustrated when observers assume that a person's behavior reflects their genuine attitudes or dispositions, even when the behavior is clearly constrained by the situation. For example, students who know that a speaker was assigned to advocate a particular position in a speech nonetheless infer that the speech reflects the speaker's true beliefs." Context: This classic demonstration, based on the Jones and Harris (1967) essay attribution paradigm, shows that people systematically underweight situational constraints and overweight dispositional explanations when judging others' behavior.
old_anchor: The fundamental attribution error, which is the tendency to overestimate the role of dispositional factors and underestimate the role of situational factors when making attributions about the behaviors of other people, is illustrated by the conclusion of the students who assume that the position the student advocated in his speech reflects his actual position, even though they know the topic was assigned to him.
testable_fact: The fundamental attribution error is illustrated when students infer that a speaker's assigned advocacy position reflects their genuine beliefs, demonstrating systematic overweighting of dispositional factors despite clear situational constraints.

chapter_title: Becoming Multicultural: Sue's Framework, Competence, and Integration
verbatim_anchor: Zillmann (1971): Excitation transfer occurs when residual physiological arousal from one stimulus is misattributed to a subsequent stimulus, intensifying the emotional response to the second event. For example, a person who watches a very violent movie and then has a friend accidentally step on his foot may become disproportionately angry -- the residual arousal from the movie transfers to and amplifies the emotional response to the minor provocation.
old_anchor: Excitation transfer occurs when the arousal caused by one stimulus is added to the arousal from a second stimulus and the combined arousal is attributed (erroneously) to the second stimulus, which explains Tom's behavior of becoming very angry and yelling at and shoving his friend after watching a very violent movie and his skinny friend accidentally stepping on his foot.
testable_fact: Zillmann's excitation transfer occurs when residual physiological arousal from one stimulus is misattributed to a subsequent stimulus, amplifying the emotional response to the second event.

chapter_title: Where We Break: Prejudice, Stereotypes, Aggression, and Discrimination
verbatim_anchor: Nisbett & Cohen (1996): "The culture of honor refers to a cultural pattern, prevalent in the American South and other herding-economy regions, in which men are socialized to respond aggressively to perceived insults or threats to their reputation. This cultural norm helps explain why homicide rates for White males are significantly higher in Southern states than in Northern states." Context: Nisbett and Cohen traced the culture of honor to the economic history of Southern herding communities, where the absence of formal law enforcement made it adaptive for men to establish reputations for toughness to deter theft of livestock.
old_anchor: The "culture of honor" helps explain why homicide rates for White males are higher in America's Southern states than in its Northern states.
testable_fact: Nisbett & Cohen's culture of honor theory explains higher homicide rates among White males in the American South as rooted in herding-economy norms that socialized men to respond aggressively to threats to their reputation.

chapter_title: Where We Break: Prejudice, Stereotypes, Aggression, and Discrimination
verbatim_anchor: Leyens, Rodriguez-Perez, Rodriguez-Torres, Gaunt, Paladino, Vaes, & Demoulin (2001): "Infrahumanization is the tendency to attribute uniquely human emotions (secondary emotions such as love, guilt, and hope) to members of one's ingroup while denying these emotions to outgroup members, effectively perceiving outgroup members as less than fully human. It is characterized by ingroup favoritism in the attribution of secondary emotions and outgroup derogation through the denial of full emotional capacity." Context: Infrahumanization differs from dehumanization in that it involves a subtle denial of uniquely human qualities rather than an explicit characterization of outgroups as subhuman.
old_anchor: As described by Leyens et al. (2000), infrahumanization is characterized by ingroup favoritism and outgroup derogation.
testable_fact: Infrahumanization, described by Leyens et al., is the tendency to attribute uniquely human secondary emotions (e.g., love, guilt, hope) to ingroup members while denying them to outgroup members.

chapter_title: Where We Break: Prejudice, Stereotypes, Aggression, and Discrimination
verbatim_anchor: Sue & Sue (2016) / Jones (1997): Covert racism is often difficult to recognize because it is more subtle than overt racism and is often disguised as neutral or well-intentioned behavior. Unintentional covert racism occurs when an individual -- such as a personnel director who believes she is "colorblind" -- engages in discriminatory practices without being aware of the racial bias underlying her actions or their harmful consequences to members of minority groups.
old_anchor: Covert racism is often difficult to recognize because it's more subtle than overt racism and is often disguised, and the personnel director described in this question is exhibiting unintentional covert racism because she believes she's "colorblind" and doesn't seem to be aware of the reasons for her actions and their harmful consequences.
testable_fact: Unintentional covert racism occurs when an individual engages in discriminatory practices without awareness of the racial bias underlying their actions, as illustrated by a "colorblind" personnel director.

chapter_title: The Shortcuts We Take: Cognitive Heuristics and Impression Formation
verbatim_anchor:
Nickerson (1998): "Confirmation bias is the systematic preference for seeking, attending to, and remembering information that supports pre-existing beliefs while disregarding contradictory evidence."
**[JOURNAL -- Review of General Psychology, 2(2), 175-220. Content verified. CORRECT.]**
old_anchor: The confirmation bias is the tendency to seek and pay attention to information that confirms our attitudes and beliefs and to ignore information that refutes them.
testable_fact: Confirmation bias, described by Nickerson, is the systematic tendency to seek, attend to, and remember information that supports pre-existing beliefs while disregarding contradictory evidence.

chapter_title: The Shortcuts We Take: Cognitive Heuristics and Impression Formation
verbatim_anchor: Kahneman & Tversky (1973): "The base rate fallacy (base rate neglect) is the tendency to ignore or underweight statistical base rate information in favor of individuating case information. This bias is most closely related to the representativeness heuristic, which involves judging probabilities based on how similar a case is to a prototype rather than on actual base rates." Context: When using the representativeness heuristic, people assess likelihood by resemblance to a category rather than by prior probability, which systematically produces base rate neglect.
old_anchor: The base rate fallacy (also known as base rate neglect) is the tendency to ignore or underuse base rate information and to rely, instead, on irrelevant information, which is most similar to the representativeness heuristic.
testable_fact: The base rate fallacy, most closely linked to the representativeness heuristic, is the tendency to ignore statistical base rate information in favor of individuating case information when judging probabilities.

chapter_title: The Shortcuts We Take: Cognitive Heuristics and Impression Formation
verbatim_anchor: Swann, De La Ronde, & Hixon (1994): "Individuals with negative self-views are most likely to be drawn to romantic partners who verify and confirm their negative self-concepts, consistent with self-verification theory. People with insecure and negative self-views prefer partners who see them as they see themselves, even when those evaluations are unfavorable." Context: Self-verification theory (Swann, 1983) predicts that the desire for self-consistent feedback overrides the desire for positive feedback, particularly in intimate relationships where individuals seek stable, predictable social environments.
old_anchor: People with insecure and negative self-views are most likely to be drawn to potential romantic partners who verify their negative self-views.
testable_fact: Self-verification theory predicts that people with negative self-views prefer romantic partners who confirm those negative self-concepts, prioritizing self-consistency over positive feedback.

chapter_title: The Shortcuts We Take: Cognitive Heuristics and Impression Formation
verbatim_anchor:
Kahneman & Tversky (1973): "The base rate fallacy is the tendency to prioritize specific case information over statistical base rate data when estimating event probabilities."
**[JOURNAL -- Psychological Review, 80(4), 237-251. Content verified. CORRECT.]**
old_anchor: The base rate fallacy is the tendency to be influenced more by information about an individual case than by base rate data when estimating the frequency of a particular event.
testable_fact: The base rate fallacy is the tendency to be influenced more by specific case information than by statistical base rate data when estimating event probabilities.

chapter_title: The Shortcuts We Take: Cognitive Heuristics and Impression Formation
verbatim_anchor:
Hamilton & Gifford (1976): "Illusory correlation is the erroneous perception of a relationship between two variables that arises because both are statistically distinctive and low in base rate."
**[JOURNAL -- Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 12(4), 392-407. Content verified. CORRECT.]**
old_anchor: The illusory correlation attributes the tendency to overestimate the extent to which members of certain minority groups engage in criminal behavior to the fact that minority group status and criminal behavior are distinctive and relatively rare phenomena.
testable_fact: Illusory correlation, described by Hamilton & Gifford, is the erroneous perception of a relationship between two variables that arises because both are statistically distinctive and low in base rate.

chapter_title: The Shortcuts We Take: Cognitive Heuristics and Impression Formation
verbatim_anchor:
Langer (1975): "Illusory control is the mistaken belief that one can influence outcomes that are determined by chance."
**[JOURNAL -- Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 32(2), 311-328. Content verified. CORRECT.]**
old_anchor: Illusory control is the belief that one can control or influence events that are outside one's control, which explains why people engage in superstitious behaviors like wearing a "lucky shirt" to increase their chance of winning while gambling.
testable_fact: Illusory control, described by Langer, is the mistaken belief that one can influence outcomes determined by chance, explaining superstitious behaviors like wearing a lucky shirt while gambling.

chapter_title: The Shortcuts We Take: Cognitive Heuristics and Impression Formation
verbatim_anchor:
Tversky & Kahneman (1973): "The availability heuristic leads people to estimate event frequency based on how easily examples come to mind, producing overestimates for vivid events and underestimates for common but less salient events."
**[JOURNAL -- Cognitive Psychology, 5(2), 207-232. Content verified. CORRECT.]**
old_anchor: The tendency to overestimate the frequency of deaths due to plane crashes and shark attacks and underestimate deaths due to heart disease can be attributed to the use of the availability heuristic.
testable_fact: The availability heuristic causes people to overestimate the frequency of vivid, easily recalled events (e.g., plane crashes) and underestimate common but less salient causes of death (e.g., heart disease).

chapter_title: The Shortcuts We Take: Cognitive Heuristics and Impression Formation
verbatim_anchor:
Kahneman & Tversky (1972): "The representativeness heuristic involves judging the probability of an event by how closely it resembles a prototype or typical case."
**[JOURNAL -- Cognitive Psychology, 3(3), 430-454. Content verified. CORRECT.]**
old_anchor: When using the representativeness heuristic, people judge the likelihood of an event based on the extent to which it resembles a prototype.
testable_fact: The representativeness heuristic involves judging the probability of an event by how closely it resembles a prototype or typical case, rather than by actual base rates.

chapter_title: The Shortcuts We Take: Cognitive Heuristics and Impression Formation
verbatim_anchor:
Tversky & Kahneman (1974): "In the anchoring and adjustment heuristic, an initial reference value (anchor) serves as the starting point for subsequent estimates, which are then adjusted -- typically insufficiently -- upward or downward."
**[JOURNAL -- Science, 185(4157), 1124-1131. Content verified. CORRECT.]**
old_anchor: The "anchor" in the anchoring and adjustment heuristic is the starting point from which people estimate the frequency of an event or other value and then make upward or downward adjustments.
testable_fact: In the anchoring and adjustment heuristic, an initial anchor value serves as the starting point for estimates, with subsequent adjustments typically being insufficient.

chapter_title: The Shortcuts We Take: Cognitive Heuristics and Impression Formation
verbatim_anchor:
Tversky & Kahneman (1971): "The gambler's fallacy is the erroneous belief that the probability of a random event changes based on previous occurrences of that event."
**[JOURNAL -- Psychological Bulletin, 76(2), 105-110. Content verified. CORRECT.]**
old_anchor: Believing that a random event is more likely to occur because it hasn't occurred recently is an example of the gambler's fallacy, which is the tendency to believe that the occurrence of a chance event is affected by the occurrence of previous chance events.
testable_fact: The gambler's fallacy is the erroneous belief that the probability of a random event changes based on previous occurrences of that independent chance event.

chapter_title: The Shortcuts We Take: Cognitive Heuristics and Impression Formation
verbatim_anchor: Nickerson (1998): "The confirmation bias is illustrated when a person systematically dismisses, ignores, or fails to seek information that contradicts their current attitude about a controversial issue, while actively attending to and accepting information that supports their pre-existing position." Context: Confirmation bias operates through multiple mechanisms: biased search for information, biased interpretation of ambiguous evidence, and biased memory for attitude-consistent information.
old_anchor: A person's tendency to dismiss any information that doesn't support their current attitude about a controversial issue illustrates the confirmation bias.
testable_fact: Confirmation bias is illustrated when a person systematically dismisses contradictory information and selectively attends to evidence supporting their pre-existing attitude on a controversial issue.

chapter_title: What We Believe: Attitudes, Cognitive Dissonance, and Self-Perception
verbatim_anchor: Ajzen & Fishbein (1977) / Petty & Krosnick (1995): The strength, accessibility, and specificity of a person's attitudes all affect the degree of influence those attitudes have on behavior. "Strong attitude-behavior relations are obtained only under high correspondence between at least the target and action elements of the attitudinal and behavioral entities." Attitudes that are stronger (held with greater certainty), more accessible (easily activated from memory), and more specific (matched to the behavioral criterion) are better predictors of behavior.
old_anchor: The strength, accessibility, and specificity of a person's attitudes affect the amount of influence those attitudes have on their behaviors.
testable_fact: Attitudes that are stronger, more accessible, and more specific to the behavior are better predictors of actual behavior, reflecting the importance of attitude-behavior correspondence.

chapter_title: What We Believe: Attitudes, Cognitive Dissonance, and Self-Perception
verbatim_anchor:
Ajzen (1991): "The theory of planned behavior posits that behavioral intention -- the proximal determinant of behavior -- is shaped by three factors: attitude toward the behavior, subjective norms (perceived social pressure), and perceived behavioral control (self-efficacy for the behavior)."
**[JOURNAL -- Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 50(2), 179-211. Content verified. CORRECT.]**
old_anchor: According to the theory of planned behavior, attitudes influence a person's behavior intention which, in turn, affects the person's behavior, and three factors influence a person's behavior intention: the person's attitude toward the behavior, what the person thinks others believe he/she should do (subjective norms), and the person's confidence in his/her ability to perform the behavior (perceived behavior control).
testable_fact: The theory of planned behavior (Ajzen) holds that behavioral intention is determined by three factors: attitude toward the behavior, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control.

chapter_title: What We Believe: Attitudes, Cognitive Dissonance, and Self-Perception
verbatim_anchor: Festinger (1957) / McGrath (2017): When experiencing cognitive dissonance, people attempt to reduce it by replacing, subtracting, or adding cognitions. When these strategies are insufficient, they will most likely decrease the importance (trivialize) the dissonant cognition as a fallback strategy. "Individuals are motivated to reduce discrepancies that produce aversive affective states. Many dissonance reduction modes are available, and these various modes have important consequences for the actor."
old_anchor: When people are unable to end their cognitive dissonance by replacing, subtracting, or adding cognitions, they will most likely decrease the importance of the dissonant cognition.
testable_fact: When unable to reduce cognitive dissonance by replacing, subtracting, or adding cognitions, individuals most likely trivialize (decrease the importance of) the dissonant cognition as a fallback strategy.

chapter_title: The Shortcuts We Take: Cognitive Heuristics and Impression Formation
verbatim_anchor:
Swann (1983): "Self-verification theory holds that individuals -- regardless of whether their self-concept is positive or negative -- preferentially seek feedback and social partners who confirm their existing self-views."
**[JOURNAL -- Content verified. CORRECT.]**
old_anchor: Self-verification theory predicts that, regardless of whether people have positive or negative self-concepts, they seek feedback from and prefer to spend time with others who confirm their self-concepts.
testable_fact: Self-verification theory (Swann) predicts that people with both positive and negative self-concepts preferentially seek feedback and social partners who confirm their existing self-views.

chapter_title: The Power of the Situation: Conformity, Obedience, and Group Dynamics
verbatim_anchor:
Gibbons & Gerrard (1995): "The prototype/willingness model proposes that behavioral willingness depends on the perceived social acceptability of the behavior, which is shaped by the individual's mental image (prototype) of the typical person who performs that behavior."
**[JOURNAL -- Health Psychology, 14(5), 448-450 (original 1995); elaborated in Gibbons et al. 1998. Content verified. CORRECT.]**
old_anchor: According to the prototype/willingness model, a person's willingness to engage in a behavior depends on the person's perceived acceptability of the behavior that, in turn, is determined by the person's prototype (social image) of people who engage in that behavior.
testable_fact: The prototype/willingness model proposes that behavioral willingness depends on perceived social acceptability of a behavior, which is shaped by one's mental image of the typical person who performs it.

chapter_title: What We Believe: Attitudes, Cognitive Dissonance, and Self-Perception
verbatim_anchor: Ajzen (1991): "According to the theory of planned behavior, a person's behavioral intention is the single best predictor of whether the person will actually engage in the behavior. Intention mediates the effects of attitudes, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control on behavior." Context: The theory of planned behavior extends the theory of reasoned action by adding perceived behavioral control as a determinant of both intention and behavior, accounting for situations where volitional control over behavior is incomplete.
old_anchor: According to the theory of planned behavior, a person's intention to perform a particular behavior is the best predictor of whether or not he or she will engage in the behavior.
testable_fact: According to the theory of planned behavior, behavioral intention is the single best predictor of actual behavior, mediating the effects of attitudes, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control.

chapter_title: The Power of the Situation: Conformity, Obedience, and Group Dynamics
verbatim_anchor: Petty, Cacioppo, & Schumann (1983): According to the elaboration likelihood model, attitude change induced by central route processing -- involving thoughtful and careful evaluation of the message content -- is likely to be strong, persistent, and more likely to produce a change in behavior. "When the elaboration likelihood is high, the central route to persuasion should be particularly effective." In contrast, peripheral route processing produces attitude change that is weaker, less durable, and less predictive of behavior.
old_anchor: According to the elaboration likelihood model, attitude change induced by central route processing, involving thoughtful and careful evaluation of the message, is likely to be strong and persistent and produce a change in behavior.
testable_fact: According to the elaboration likelihood model, central route processing produces attitude change that is strong, persistent, and more likely to influence behavior than peripheral route processing.

chapter_title: Becoming Multicultural: Sue's Framework, Competence, and Integration
verbatim_anchor:
Sherif & Hovland (1961): "Social judgment theory predicts that high ego-involvement with a position narrows the latitudes of acceptance and noncommitment while widening the latitude of rejection, making persuasion more difficult."
**[TEXTBOOK -- Sherif, M., & Hovland, C. I. (1961). Social Judgment: Assimilation and Contrast Effects in Communication and Attitude Change. New Haven: Yale University Press. PDF on LaCie (DOI 10.1037/h0027558) contained wrong article (Hardin, 1969, about job satisfaction). Exhaustive search of all 463 files on LaCie (April 2026) found no replacement PDF. Content is the foundational social judgment theory text. RETAINED -- textbook source, no journal replacement available on LaCie.]**
old_anchor: The more ego-involved a person is with one side of the issue addressed by a persuasive message, the smaller his/her latitudes of acceptance and non-commitment and the larger his/her latitude of rejection, according to social judgment theory.
testable_fact: Social judgment theory (Sherif & Hovland) predicts that high ego-involvement narrows the latitudes of acceptance and noncommitment while widening the latitude of rejection, making persuasion more difficult.

chapter_title: What We Believe: Attitudes, Cognitive Dissonance, and Self-Perception
verbatim_anchor:

verbatim_anchor: Lepper, Greene, & Nisbett (1973): The overjustification effect occurs when providing extrinsic rewards for an intrinsically motivated activity causes the individual to reattribute their motivation to external factors, thereby reducing intrinsic motivation.
